cim_eredeti: Gen Z Turns to AI to Navigate Homebuying
szoveg_eredeti:
Homebuyers are using AI to estimate mortgage payments, compare neighborhoods and calculate closing costs, with 32% of Gen Z consumers using the technology for homebuying research, Bank of America found.

Real estate firms are struggling to turn AI pilots into measurable results, with 90% testing the technology but only 5% meeting their AI goals and more than 60% unprepared to scale, according to JLL.

Mortgage lenders face new AI oversight standards as Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac introduce governance frameworks covering accountability, monitoring and human oversight.

First-time buyers are turning to artificial intelligence to shortlist homes, often before they call an agent or visit a lender’s site. The real estate industry is adapting.

Case in point: Bank of America found in its 2026 Homebuyer Insights Report that 20% of prospective buyers and current homeowners used AI tools or chatbots for homebuying research in the past year. The share is 28% for millennials. It is 32% for Gen Z.

Bank of America’s report shows the top use was money. Among AI users, 57% estimated affordability, mortgage payments or closing costs. Another 55% used AI to learn about the process. A further 52% researched neighborhoods, market trends or property values.

Matt Vernon, Bank of America’s head of consumer lending, said AI is becoming “a meaningful first step in the homebuying journey.” The report finds that 55% of prospective buyers prefer a human for touring homes. It finds that 54% want human help with legal or contractual advice.

Bank of America also reports rising confidence. This year, 32% of respondents feel more confident in their ability to buy, up from 27% last year. At the same time, 53% now favor buying over renting. That is the first majority since 2023.

Real estate companies are racing to meet that buyer.

A World Economic Forum article says real estate is in its biggest transformation in a generation. It compares the pace of AI adoption to the early days of the internet. JLL research cited in the article shows that 90% of real estate companies now test AI. Three years ago, the share was 5%.

The same research finds that only 5% of real estate companies report meeting their AI goals. It finds that more than 60% are not ready to scale beyond pilots. The article calls this the pilot trap.

The article names leadership as the difference. Companies with a C-suite sponsor for their tech program are three times more likely to have a successful tech program. Successful programs are better resourced in AI skills. A JLL study finds that only 33% of workers feel adequately trained on AI.

The article calls AI a people challenge, not a technology problem. While the mortgage industry is writing its own rules.

An Urban Institute article says AI already works across most stages of mortgage finance. Those stages include marketing, underwriting, valuation, fraud detection, servicing and loss mitigation. Urban says effective AI can speed underwriting, lower origination costs and make routine servicing faster.

Freddie Mac and Fannie Mae introduced AI governance frameworks in early 2026. The industry’s standards body, MISMO, released a toolkit in June. Urban says the toolkit is voluntary and aligned with a federal AI risk framework from the National Institute of Standards and Technology. Urban calls Freddie Mac’s bulletin the most prescriptive of the three.

Urban says each framework asks lenders to know where they use AI. It says each asks lenders to assign accountability and monitor results. It says all three keep a human in the loop.

Urban says lenders should judge human and AI teamwork by two results. The first is more people becoming homeowners. The second is more of them staying homeowners. Urban also lists faster, more accurate matches between borrowers and homes. Urban notes that none of the frameworks yet requires lenders to show those outcomes.

Urban says Colorado’s revised law on automated decisions takes effect Jan. 1. Urban has launched an initiative on AI in mortgage finance.

The buyer’s AI is already in the room before the agent, the lender or the portal. The firms that train their people and prove their results will earn a place in that conversation.
